name: Representativeness heuristic
statement: Representativeness is a proposed mechanism rather than a finding: people are said to judge probability by resemblance, and the errors it was coined to explain replicate better than it does.
meaning: Kahneman and Tversky proposed that people answer a question about probability by answering a question about similarity instead. Representativeness is the degree to which a case resembles the category it might have come from, or an outcome resembles the process that might have produced it. Resemblance takes no account of how common a category is, how large a sample is, or how reliable the evidence is. Judgements built on it should therefore go wrong in specific ways, and the 1974 review names six: insensitivity to prior probability of outcomes, insensitivity to sample size, misconceptions of chance, insensitivity to predictability, the illusion of validity and misconceptions of regression. Five of the six have entries here. Prior probability sits at the base rate fallacy, no. 37, and sample size at no. 229. Misconceptions of chance are split between the gambler's fallacy, no. 25, and the clustering illusion, no. 60. The illusion of validity is no. 188 and regression is no. 248. Insensitivity to predictability has none. The conjunction fallacy, no. 75, arrived in 1983 and is not on the 1974 list at all. What is at issue in this entry is the shared explanation, not any one of the errors.

origin.note: "Subjective Probability: A Judgment of Representativeness" ran eleven problems on birth sequences, sampling distributions and posterior probabilities. That count is the replication's, because the 1972 paper itself could not be opened. The prediction studies followed in Psychological Review in 1973, and Science carried the summary on 27 September 1974. Neither the 1972 nor the 1973 paper could be read on 21 September 2026, so figures attributed to them here are read off the 1974 review, the 1983 conjunction paper, Kahneman's Nobel lecture or the two replications.

evidence: The 1974 review sets out the case. Told that a description had been drawn from a group of 70 engineers and 30 lawyers, or from 30 engineers and 70 lawyers, subjects produced much the same probability judgements in both conditions. Bayes's rule puts the ratio of the odds at (.7/.3) squared, or 5.44. Given a description written to carry no information, they answered .5 whichever mix they had been told about. Given no description at all they answered .7 and .3, which is correct. Asked whether a hospital with about 45 births a day or one with about 15 recorded more days on which over 60% of babies were boys, 21 undergraduates said the larger, 21 said the smaller and 53 said about the same. Asked which sample was stronger evidence about an urn, 4 red of 5 drawn or 12 red of 20, most chose the first, though the correct posterior odds are 8 to 1 and 16 to 1. The direct evidence for the mechanism comes from a different design, in which one group ranks outcomes by how far a person resembles each and another group ranks the same outcomes by probability. Kahneman's Nobel lecture gives a correlation of .97 between the mean representativeness and mean probability rankings for Tom W., against a rank correlation of -.65 between representativeness rankings and estimated base rates. The Linda figures belong to a particular version, and are usually quoted without it. In Tversky and Kahneman's 1983 paper, 88 undergraduates at the University of British Columbia ranked eight statements about Linda by resemblance, and 85% produced the order feminist, feminist bank teller, bank teller. Other groups ranked the same eight statements by probability. Violations of the conjunction rule ran at 89% among the statistically naive, 90% among the informed and 85% among the sophisticated, and the correlation between mean probability and mean representativeness ranks was .98 for Linda. Kahneman's lecture gives that correlation as .99, and pairs 85% for representativeness with 89% for probability. The 89% is the naive group's figure in the 1983 table, and the lecture does not say which group it is quoting.

replication.headline: The chance and sampling problems of 1972 repeat almost intact, eight of nine in a preregistered replication, while the prediction studies of 1973 come apart, with two of six supported.
replication.detail: Mayiwar, Wan, Loehre and Feldman ran the first direct replication of the 1972 paper, on 623 participants, from 683 recruited on Amazon MTurk through CloudResearch, each answering five of the nine problems. Eight of the nine came out as the original did. Of the 343 who saw the birth sequences, 293 rated BGBBBB less probable than GBGBBG, h = 0.79, 95% CI [0.68, 0.89], and 303 rated BBBGGG less probable than GBBGBG, h = 0.87, 95% CI [0.77, 0.98]. Of the 360 who saw the high-school problem, 336 chose the class whose proportions matched the population, h = 1.05, 95% CI [0.95, 1.15]. Of the 348 who saw the randomness problem, 223 called a non-uniform distribution more probable than a uniform one, h = 0.29, 95% CI [0.18, 0.39]. The paper's running text puts all three denominators at 343 and prints the last effect as h = 0.28 with the interval from the birth sequences, so the figures here are taken from its design, descriptives and comparison tables. Estimated sampling distributions did not differ between samples of 10, 100 and 1,000 in any of three scenarios. On the sample-size problems the replication reports that the count choosing the correct answer exceeded half in none of the six comparisons. In three of them, the more extreme condition of the investigator problem and both conditions of the disease problem, Bayes factors favoured a real effect over the null. The one failure was the binomial posterior-probability problem, where the original ordering of judgements did not reappear. With the deck at two to one, estimates for the 5:1 sample did not differ from those for 4:2, 8:4 or 40:20. With the deck at five to one, the 5:1 sample beat only 8:4. The authors note that the 40:20 sample is in fact much the stronger evidence. The 1973 paper fared worse. Chan, supervised by Feldman, put its studies to 801 US participants on Prolific, targeting 800 and taking the extra completions the platform sent. Two of the six were supported, two mixed and two not. The engineer-lawyer study was one of the failures. The base-rate manipulation produced a main effect of F(1, 789) = 102.77, p < .001, eta-squared = .081, and the description written to be worthless drew a mean of 64.27% in the high-engineer condition against 32.65% in the low, which is base-rate use rather than base-rate neglect. The outcome-ranking design weakened too. Across six descriptions the replication obtained similarity-probability correlations of .75, .55, .08, .01, -.16 and -.28, only the first of which reached significance, against original values of .88 to .97 that are quoted from the replication's own comparison table rather than from the 1973 paper.

study.cite: Mayiwar, L., Wan, K. H., Løhre, E., & Feldman, G. (2025). Revisiting representativeness heuristic classic paradigms: Replication and extensions of nine experiments in Kahneman and Tversky (1972). Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology, 78(4), 707-730.

limits: No multi-site or multi-laboratory replication was located. Crossref, PubMed, the Open Science Framework's preprint index and the Many Labs and Registered Replication Report catalogues were searched on 21 September 2026 and returned none, so the record is two single-sample online studies. Both originals stayed shut on that date. Elsevier's page for the 1972 paper answers with a Cloudflare block, and Springer sells a shorter reprint and shows only its abstract. APA's landing page for the 1973 paper answers with an Imperva bot block rather than a paywall notice. Semantic Scholar records the 1972 paper as closed and holds no record at all for the 1973 DOI, and Unpaywall lists no repository copy for either. The 1974 review was read in the copy hosted by the University of California, Irvine. The version of record of the 1972 replication was not read either. SAGE's page and the University of Hong Kong repository both answer with a Cloudflare challenge, not a paywall, so its figures come from the accepted manuscript the authors deposited at the Open Science Framework, which carries the published title and abstract. The 1973 replication is the weaker of the two documents. It is an undergraduate thesis, and it says that its data were collected before in-principle acceptance, which led the editor to lower Peer Community's level of control from six to two. It sits beside the Stage 1 registered report that Rima-Maria Rahal recommended for in-principle acceptance on 31 May 2024. That Stage 1 report is listed at N = 1,309, and its results section says the 1,309 cases were simulated in Qualtrics and would later be replaced by real data at a sample of 800. Entry no. 248 sets out what follows from that. No Stage 2 report was located on 21 September 2026. Crossref holds one record under the Peer Community prefix for this project and no later one, and the project's storage holds a Stage 1 folder and a thesis folder and nothing else. The Peer Community article page and its files both opened to an ordinary request on that date. The thesis's item-level correlations each rest on nine fields of specialisation and are printed as r(7). The intervals include [-.80, .47] and [-.66, .67]. Ranges that wide settle neither the presence nor the absence of the original correlation. That design is the one test on the record that bears on the mechanism rather than on an error, which is why Kahneman and Tversky called it their most direct evidence. The same searches found no study that sets resemblance against a competing account of the same judgements in one sample.
misreadings: The commonest error is to treat representativeness as a result. It is an explanation, it has been disputed for more than thirty years, and the errors it explains have mostly held while it has not. In 1996 Kahneman and Tversky defended it against Gigerenzer's earlier charge that heuristics are "largely undefined concepts and can post hoc be used to explain almost everything". Their answer was that representativeness, like similarity, can be assessed experimentally, so it need not be defined a priori. They added that the outcome-ranking evidence had not been challenged. Gigerenzer replied in the same issue that notions such as representativeness "remain vague, undefined, and unspecified" as to what elicits them and what processes underlie them, and that post hoc one of them can be fitted to almost any experimental result. Kahneman later granted in his Nobel lecture that the 1974 article contained no definition of a judgemental heuristic, and that heuristics had been described at various times as principles, as processes, or as sources of cues. He and Frederick supplied one in 2002, attribute substitution, which has its own entry at no. 202. The outcome-ranking evidence has since been challenged, by the 1973 replication above. The second error is reading base-rate neglect as total. Koehler's review concluded that base rates are almost always used and that how much depends on task structure and representation. Kahneman and Tversky granted as much in 1996, writing that subjects sometimes use stated base rates far more than they did in the original engineer-lawyer study, though generally less than Bayes's rule requires. The base rate fallacy entry, no. 37, carries the figures. The third error is taking the conjunction fallacy and the gambler's fallacy as tests of representativeness. Each has its own entry, at no. 75 and no. 25, and its own replication record, and each survives accounts that make no use of resemblance. Barbey and Sloman argue for one such account, that judgements go wrong when a problem obscures the nested sets it contains. They report that Sloman and colleagues found almost nobody committing the conjunction fallacy when the options were drawn as Euler circles. The fourth is quoting the 1978 medical study as settled fact about doctors. Barbey and Sloman put its proportion of Bayesian answers at 18%, against 5% for Eddy's breast cancer problem, and the base rate fallacy entry records how few people it tested.

sources.text: Kahneman, D., & Tversky, A. (1972). Subjective probability: A judgment of representativeness. Cognitive Psychology, 3(3), 430-454. The paper that introduced the term. Not read on 21 September 2026: Elsevier's article page answers with a Cloudflare block, Springer's shorter reprint shows only its abstract behind a subscription, Semantic Scholar records it as closed and Unpaywall lists no repository copy. No figure attributed to it here was read in it.

Kahneman, D., & Tversky, A. (1973). On the psychology of prediction. Psychological Review, 80(4), 237-251. Source of the engineer-lawyer and Tom W. studies. Not read on 21 September 2026: APA's DOI landing page and PsycNET answer with an Imperva bot block rather than a paywall notice, Semantic Scholar holds no record for the DOI, Europe PMC holds none, and Unpaywall lists no repository copy. Its bibliographic record was verified at Crossref.

Tversky, A., & Kahneman, D. (1974). Judgment under uncertainty: Heuristics and biases. Science, 185(4157), 1124-1131. Read in full in the copy hosted at the University of California, Irvine; the source for the 5.44 odds ratio, the .7 and .3 answers, the 21, 21 and 53 hospital counts, the 8 to 1 and 16 to 1 urn odds and the six errors listed above.

Tversky, A., & Kahneman, D. (1983). Extensional versus intuitive reasoning: The conjunction fallacy in probability judgment. Psychological Review, 90(4), 293-315. Read in full in the copy hosted at the University of California, San Diego; the source for the 88 UBC undergraduates, the 85% resemblance order, the 89%, 90% and 85% violation rates in its Table 1 and the .98 correlation.

Kahneman, D. (2002). Maps of bounded rationality: A perspective on intuitive judgment and choice. Prize Lecture, 8 December 2002. Read in full as the PDF at nobelprize.org; the source for the .97 and -.65 correlations for Tom W., the .99, 85% and 89% figures for Linda, the admission that the 1974 article defined no heuristic, and the 2002 definition of attribute substitution.

Mayiwar, L., Wan, K. H., Løhre, E., & Feldman, G. (2025). Revisiting representativeness heuristic classic paradigms: Replication and extensions of nine experiments in Kahneman and Tversky (1972). Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology, 78(4), 707-730. Read in full as the accepted manuscript deposited at the Open Science Framework, which carries the published title and abstract; the source for every 1972 replication figure above and for the count of eleven problems in the target article. SAGE's version of record and the University of Hong Kong repository copy both answer with a Cloudflare challenge, not a paywall.

Chan, H. C. (2024). Representativeness heuristic in intuitive predictions: Replication Registered Report of problems reviewed in Kahneman and Tversky (1973). Undergraduate thesis, Department of Psychology, University of Hong Kong, supervised by Gilad Feldman, dated 30 April 2024. Read in full as the deposited PDF; the source for the 801 participants, the engineer-lawyer figures, the six similarity-probability correlations and the statement that data collection preceded in-principle acceptance.

Chan, H. C., & Feldman, G. (2024). Representativeness heuristic in intuitive predictions: Replication Registered Report of problems reviewed in Kahneman and Tversky (1973) [Stage 1], version 5. Read in full as the deposited PDF; the source for the statement that the 1,309 cases reported in it were simulated in Qualtrics and would later be replaced by real data at a sample of 800.

Rahal, R.-M. (2024). The Representativeness Heuristic Revisited: Registered Replication Report of Kahneman and Tversky (1973). Peer Community in Registered Reports, 31 May 2024. The in-principle acceptance of the Stage 1 protocol, not a recommendation of results. Read in full at the Peer Community site on 21 September 2026, which served the page and its files without challenge; the abstract it carries opens with a note that its method and results were written from a simulated dataset.

Chan, H. C., & Feldman, G. (2024). Reply to 3rd RNR decision letter reviews #609: Kahneman and Tversky (1973) replication and extension. Annex filed with Peer Community in Registered Reports. Read in full as the PDF served by the Peer Community site; the source for the target of 800 participants on Prolific and for the authors' undertaking to keep any completions the platform sent beyond it.

Kahneman, D., & Tversky, A. (1996). On the reality of cognitive illusions. Psychological Review, 103(3), 582-591. Read in full in the copy hosted at the University of California, San Diego; the source for the reply that representativeness can be assessed experimentally and need not be defined a priori, for the claim that the outcome-ranking evidence had not been challenged, and for the concession about stated base rates.

Gigerenzer, G. (1996). On narrow norms and vague heuristics: A reply to Kahneman and Tversky (1996). Psychological Review, 103(3), 592-596. Read in full as the author's copy in the Max Planck Society repository; the source for the "vague, undefined, and unspecified" wording and the post hoc charge. It answers Kahneman and Tversky's paper above, and is not the paper they were answering.

Barbey, A. K., & Sloman, S. A. (2007). Base-rate respect: From ecological rationality to dual processes. Behavioral and Brain Sciences, 30(3), 241-254. Read in full as the PDF hosted by the authors' laboratory; the source for the nested-sets account, the 18% and 5% Bayesian answer rates, and the report of Sloman and colleagues on Euler circles.

Koehler, J. J. (1996). The base rate fallacy reconsidered: Descriptive, normative, and methodological challenges. Behavioral and Brain Sciences, 19(1), 1-17. Read in full as the scan hosted at fitelson.org; the source for the finding that base rates are almost always used and that their use depends on task structure and representation.
